August 16, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Motion No. 9
That Bill C-130 be amended by adding immediately after line 43 at page 3 the following:
"7. For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to apply to lands, resources, and waters claims by aboriginal peoples under an aboriginal claim."
Motion No. 10
That Bill C-130 be amended by adding immediately after line 43 at page 3 the following:
"7. For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall affect programs to protect the environment or conservation of land, resources and waters."
Motion No. 11
That Bill C-130 be amended by adding immediately after line 43 at page 3 the following:
"7. For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to affect or preclude the continuation of existing or the establishment of new special adjustment programs to help firms or workers adjust to the changes brought about by the implementation of the Agreement."
Motion No. 12
That Bill C-130 be amended by adding immediately after lines 43 at page 3 the following:
"7. For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to affect or preclude the continuation of existing or the establishment of new regional development programs."
Motion No. 13
That Bill C-130 be amended by adding immediately after line 43 at page 3 the following:
"7. For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to affect the continuation of existing or the establishment of new Canadian social programs, including medicare, unemployment insurance, daycare, pensions, minimum wage laws, labour laws and maternity benefits."
Motion No. 14
That Bill C-130 be amended by adding immediately after line 43 at page 3 the following:
"7. For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to affect or preclude the continuation of existing or the establishment of new cultural programs by future Canadian governments."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this group of amendments that were moved will put the Government to a test. It will challenge the assertions that they have made over the past two years. The important parts of the Canadian national fabric; environment, aboriginal rights, regional development programs, cultural programs, are in no way affected by this agreement. We have heard the guarantees, assurances, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). That great counterfeiter has provided every kind of guarantee that one could ask for.
Now they have a chance to prove it by voting for these amendments. Now we will really see if they are prepared to live up to their word. There is a very important precedent for supporting these amendments. The Government said that during the course of the last month or two, because of a concern raised in the country about the issue of water, they would move an amendment to the legislation for greater certainty. For greater certainty they moved an amendment to ensure that water was excluded in the legislation.
We have here five amendments which say that for greater certainty we want to ensure that cultural programs, regional
development programs, and adjustment programs will not be affected. So if the Conservatives can support an amendment for greater certainty on water, then surely they will have to support these amendments for greater certainty on issues that have raised similar doubts and skepticism in the minds of many Canadians. It is very simple. They vote for these amendments, they support them, then, in part they will have taken away much of the doubt that exists, so they can say that at least in the legislation we have made our case clear and we know.
In my own generous, charitable way I am trying to help the Government. I want to give Government Members the means by which they can convince Canadians that they are prepared to stand by their word.
I have a suspicion, though I do not want to be too skeptical, that Government Members may not vote for these amendments. If they do not vote for them, then we will know that all those assurances are simply the kind of misrepresentation we have had from the time this agreement was first announced. We will not be able to trust them any longer.
I would like to deal with one particular amendment. My colleagues will deal with environmental issues, social policy and aboriginal rights, but I want to deal with adjustment. We know how important that is. The Economic Council of Canada has indicated that some 186,000 workers will be dislocated by this agreement.
Before the committee we heard testimony from the food processing industry, one of Canada's largest employers, indicating that close to 60,000 workers could lose their jobs as a result of the free trade agreement. The printing industry, a highly skilled industry, a small business industry based in every city across Canada, estimated that 10,000 workers could lose their jobs. The same is true for the textile, clothing, machine and electrical fabrication industries.
There was very substantial testimony from members of industry groups indicating that they will be directly affected by this agreement. Companies will close down. Workers will lose their jobs. It is very clear that adjustment programs will be required.
What has been so curious is why the Government changed its mind about so-called adjustment programs. The Prime Minister, before a big convention in Ottawa, said that there will be a big adjustment program, not to worry. The then Minister of Employment and Immigration indicated that there could be up to half a million workers affected. All of a sudden, about a week later, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister started changing their tune. We are used to that. We are used to them changing their tune on a 24-hour cycle, but surely not on something as important as someone's job being put at stake.
August 16, 1988

We began to understand why this is so. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance recognized that bringing in the kind of adjustment programs that would be required would be contrary to the agreement itself. They recognized that the Americans would exercise their right under the agreement to take trade action, according to U.S. trade law, against any industry.
As an example, we know that the applications for assistance by various industries under our regional development programs are now being screened by the Department of External Affairs to determine whether or not they live up to the conditions of the agreement. Already, before the trade deal is even in place, bureaucrats are providing a filter to determine if programs passed by this Parliament, in its sovereign right to help regions or workers, are acceptable. They are being censored by DRIE and by the Western Diversification Agency. Those agencies admit to that.
In the committee, I posed a question to Ambassador Ritchie who was testifying before the committee. I said that the assurances given by the Government were that the adjustment programs would not be affected. Ambassador Ritchie went on to say, as recorded in issue 22:24 of committee testimony, the following:
"The difficulty would of course arise with targeted assistance to particular firms or particular industries. There the jurisprudence, if one can qualify it in such a way, is ambiguous and would leave open the distinct possibility that certain forms of assistance could be attacked under Canadian law or under American law.
In addition to that, it should perhaps be noted that there are a number of
other forms of adjustment assistance or measures that could be presented as
adjustment assistance which would be contrary to the agreement-"
The most knowledgeable bureaucrat, the one who negotiated the agreement, now admits that adjustment programs for industries would in fact be contrary to the agreement. That seems to be a pretty compelling argument for how we are limiting our independence as a Parliament. Programs already passed by Parliament will be subject to the discipline of the trade agreement with the Americans.
We saw a very clear example of that in the softwood lumber case. The Americans challenged the right of provincial governments to impose a certain royalty scheme because they said that it was an unfair form of government subsidy. The Government of Canada agreed with them, and as a result, we imposed a $600-million tax on ourselves.
Perhaps more significantly, by accepting that judgment and not challenging it at the GATT, we accepted the precedent that this kind of direct assistance to industries could be considered an unfair trade act on behalf of Canada. We surrendered before the battle started. We gave up those rights before the battle even began. That precedent established in the softwood lumber case is now being applied to all other kinds of Canadian exports.
Let me give Hon. Members another example that should give real cause for concern. Under the American implementing legislation that is being examined by Congress today, Congress
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
is taking upon itself new powers to monitor all Canadian exports to determine if there is a subsidy. The Congress will not require U.S. industries to do the work themselves, the U.S. Government will pay for it. By monitoring it, it is prepared to take action against any Canadian exports. The Congress has acquired a brand new trade power.
One of the great ironies of the free trade deal is that after two and a half years of negotiation, we are ending up with tougher U.S. laws. The writing is on the wall. If there is any attempt by the federal or provincial governments to provide direct assistance to specific industries to meet the needs of the dislocation that will be caused by the trade agreement, we will be subject to American attack and the Americans will have the power and precedent of the agreement to point to. That is why they are backing off. That is why they are in retreat on this issue.
This amendment, along with the several others in the grouping on culture and social programs, is here to put the legislation to a test. If there is any question in the minds of Canadians about just how strong and unalterable an impact this trade agreement will have on the right of Canadians to make decisions for themselves, the test will be tonight when this vote is taken. When Government Members rise to vote against this amendment, it will be a confession of guilt. It will be an admission that we have already surrendered our right as the Parliament of Canada to take actions to support workers and industries that will need assistance to deal with the dislocation that this agreement will cause.
There can be no clearer example of how we will restrict and restrain our right as a Parliament, as a government and as a society to make choices for ourselves. The victims of the trade agreement will be prevented from getting decent assistance because the Government has already sold its soul. Yet we know how crucial this kind of assistance can be.
In 1971-72, when President Nixon brought in a surcharge on Canadian taxes, we introduced the Employment Support Act which provided assistance for something like 5,000 to 6,000 Canadian companies to meet the American challenge. It kept them in business, it kept their operations going and it allowed them to survive. It was a very successful program. It has now been put in abeyance by this Government.
The Canadian Industrial Renewal Board was designed to protect direct assistance to the footwear and textile industries to modernize and buy new machinery. Again, it was a successful program and was so considered by the North-South Institute, an objective institute. What did this Government do? It cancelled the program. It let it run out.
The ILAP Program allowed for a combination of assistance to communities affected by labour problems. In the throes of the downturn of the automobile industry in southern Ontario, it kept automobile communities alive. It allowed the people to keep their jobs and to bring new industry in. What did this Government do? It cancelled the program.

August 16, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Once again, we go back to the thesis that this is a Government that is trying to introduce, under the guise of a trade Bill, its kind of 19th century economic philosophy. That is, to not permit the Canadian Government to offer decent, constructive, productive support for its own citizens. They borrowed the Republican-Regeanite philosophy from the U.S. and are trying to entrench it in a Bill and an international agreement.
The group of amendments I brought forward, which you will hear a great deal about tonight, are the ultimate test. They will show the Canadian people who is right and who is wrong in this debate. What we say is that the Government has sold out the right of Canadians to make decisions for themselves.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite the heavy and very expensive flow of propaganda which has come out of the Government, despite the huffing and blustering which has come from the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) and his Parliamentary Secretary, we in this Party, and a great many other Canadians, know this trade agreement is much more than merely a commercial transaction. It is in fact changing the very direction in which Canadian society has gone.
It is interesting to note how very quickly the U.S. administration and the Congress gave their sanction to this trade agreement. Why not? Like the "Open sesame" door, this agreement has opened to the United States all the rich natural resources of Canada. In a sense, we could describe it as one of the biggest giveaways in the history of the western world.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: You will hear from me again, too. We have to keep you honest.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
No wonder the great business corporations and those who speak for them love the agreement. Yet what about other Canadians? That is who we are talking about tonight, other Canadians who care about the environment, Canadians of aboriginal ancestry, Canadians who know they are not in a strong position to survive as employees in the new kind of society that this trade agreement will bring about, and I will describe that in a moment.
What this trade agreement seeks to do, to put it one way, is to deify the market-place. If you are a person who is ruthlessly competitive, highly entrepreneurial, if you are at all times market driven in your motives, then you may survive the stiff, vigorous U.S. competition. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) has said on more than one occasion, yes, we Canadians can compete. The trouble is that in those areas where we have been successful in competing, we have had our foot stamped on in a way that still hurts.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) mentioned the softwood lumber deal. There we were competing successfully and we know what happened. The penalty we paid because we competed successfully has now been written into this agreement and we have to live with it for
all time. I want to tell you that many Canadians with whom I speak tell me that they do not want an American market driven, commercial type of society in Canada. Many feel we have too much of that already. Certainly many of Canada's aboriginal peoples feel that way about the trade agreement. That is why the Assembly of First Nations rejected it outright. They oppose it as forcefully as they can, knowing they do not have a big voice in the Canadian political system. They have neither political nor economic power, but we give them all credit possible for the efforts they make on behalf of the First Nations and their people.
The Native Council of Canada has many serious reservations about this trade agreement. I quote to you from the committee hearings when the Assembly of First Nations appeared. They pointed out that the Government of Canada has gone to great lengths to enable people designated as nationals of the U.S. and U.S. citizens or corporations to have all the benefits and all of the protection anyone could want to operate in Canada. They may do whatever they wish with respect to trade, investment, buying and selling energy, raw resources, setting up manufacturing plants, establishing outlets for goods and services, or anything in the field of commerce. The Government has conveyed these and all other kinds of rights to people over whom Canada has absolutely no control or jurisdiction. These people are protected by this agreement, while at the same time the rights of First Nations in Canada have not been defined despite the fact they are spelled out as specific rights in Section 35 of the Constitution of Canada.
Since my time is very brief I want to limit myself to only two points and then conclude by stating to the House why we need in Bill C-130 a non-derogation clause for aboriginal peoples as proposed by my hon. friend from Winnipeg-Fort Garry in Motion No. 9.
Point number one is that a totally market driven economy can be very threatening and damaging to many, and none more so than to the aboriginal peoples of Canada. A U.S. magazine specializing in trade matters and economic issues said in a very recent issue, in explaining the Canada-U.S. trade agreement to its readers in the U.S., that as this agreement evolves, choices would expand and prices would fall for consumers in both countries as Canada becomes the equivalent of the fifty-first state. That means our goods in Canada will have to be produced more cheaply in order to be sold in the U.S. Quite obviously that means a downward pressure on wages, on benefits, on various forms of government assistance to people, communities and fledgling enterprises.
That is clearly threatening to Canada's aboriginal peoples. There may be some Canadians who say, well, a good thing, too, because we give them too much. We are too concerned. However, I tell you that there are no well informed Canadians who take that position. There are Canadians who realize that our economic debt, our economic rent to the first citizens of this country is enormous. There are still a majority of Canadians who care about human rights and who care about trying to establish as much equity as it is possible to establish in a modern society.
August 16, 1988

I know that those who have been educated, trained and conditioned to live and survive in a market driven society may do well. However, there are a great many others who are going to fall by the wayside. We in the Liberal Party are concerned about those people, and my hon. friend from Winnipeg-Fort Garry has talked about that already. Marginal firms and marginal workers, when confronted with intensified competitive forces coming from the U.S., will not be able to survive. Many of those Canadians are going to be native people. They are already less well educated than the population at large, less well trained. Already they are struggling to make it in Canadian society. They are going to find life ever so much more difficult, ever so much tougher in the American-type market driven society which the Government wants to force down our throats. I say no, and many Canadians say no.
I wish the Government would give the people of Canada the opportunity to decide before we pursue this folly any further. There is an old hymn that you may remember which says there is a wideness in God's mercy like the wideness of the sea. Be that as it may, I want to tell you, Sir, that the god of the market-place has no affection for anyone except the most successful, the most competitive, the most aggressive. The aboriginal peoples of Canada have every right to fear their place in a so-called new-right market driven American type of commercial society. The Canada-U.S. agreement is going to put major decisions respecting Canada's economy and its political decisions in the hands of the market-place, and I say that that is frightening.
My second point is that this agreement paves the way for the mass influx of American capital to gain even more control over vast sectors of mining, petroleum, and other resource sectors of the Canadian economy. While it may be true, as the Government has stated and argued, that existing land claims are grandfathered and are in no way threatened by the trade agreement, it is clear that the trade agreement is entirely silent about future agreements. Large areas of Canada rich in oil and gas are still subject to outstanding aboriginal title. Canada has no right to negotiate the allocation or management of these resources until such time as a valid treaty or agreement between the first nations affected and the Crown have been concluded. Anything less, Sir, would amount to theft.
The cash and the benefits from land claims are entitlements which cede from large tracts of traditional territory given to Canada. These entitlements must never ever be regarded as subsidies. Yet, I can imagine that when these entitlements are used to start aboriginal type of businesses and these businesses begin in some way to penetrate the American market, which the Government promises is going to be open to more Canadians, agents from the U.S. Department of Commerce will begin to smell around for subsidization. We will have many of those agents in Canada. They will be searching out subsidization in
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
exactly the same way as the CIA and FBI are constantly searching out communism.
I conclude simply by saying that we must have this nonderogation clause for aboriginal people. I plead with the House to put it in Bill C-130 for greater certainty.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us a set of five motions which, in a certain sense, attempt to set out as an objective or a certainty with respect to this trade deal something which is in fact very much threatened by the trade deal. In that sense they are strange motions. They are potentially contradictory motions. They are motions which I wish the Conservatives would confound us by adopting and then proving in the future that their adoption actually demonstrated that these were facts, once adopted.
However, in practice that is not the way it is going to be. In practice the various motions which are put forward here attempt to present some kind of protection for aboriginal land claims, some kind of protection for environmental or conservation programs, protection for new special adjustment programs to help workers or firms adjust to the changes brought about by this agreement. The motions suggest that regional development programs will be protected, that social programs, including medicare, unemployment insurance, pensions, minimum wage laws, and labour laws will be protected as well as new cultural programs.
Would that it could be so, Mr. Speaker. Would that it could be somehow in this terrible trade deal, simply by passing these motions, an established fact that these protections were provided. In fact, that cannot be done. It is not possible to do because the agreement itself, in fundamental ways, threatens each and every part of the areas which these motions are meant to protect.
I would like to mention the heart-felt speech of the Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) whose sincerity no one in this House can possibly doubt when he speaks of aboriginal land claims. I hope very much that the Conservatives will take his speech seriously and put that clause into the Bill even though the agreement contains such threats to aboriginal land claims. It includes the threat that all local governments including, therefore, local aboriginal governments, must not offer preferences, must not have the freedom to set economic policies which will be contrary to national treatment of United States firms.
I want to talk about three of the motions within this set. First, I want to talk about Motion No. 10 which says:
"For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall affect programs to protect
the environment or conservation of land, resources and waters."
It is absolutely clear, as we found out from expert testimony in committee, that protection of water cannot simply and completely be protected by an amendment to the Act. In fact, the Liberal Party has been arguing that very strongly and I am, therefore, a little surprised to see this put forward here.

August 16, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
With respect to conservation of resources, under changes which are made as a direct consequence of this agreement we will be forced to export our resources and to export our energy even when we face situations of shortage in this country. That is a fact which no one can deny. It is a fact which the Conservative Party should, if it has enough honesty within it still, stand up and admit.
I believe that the threat to environmental programs under this agreement is immense. Under this agreement for five to seven years we will negotiate subsidies.
It does not say certain subsidies and therefore includes subsidies which are provided to assist industries in this country to become environmentally viable and stop polluting rivers and lakes as a consequence of the assistance with which they are provided. That is very much at risk as a consequence of this agreement.

He cannot possibly say that these will not be negotiated. All he can say is that he can hope they will not be negotiated. I am not sure if many Conservatives share that hope. That particular motion is useful and important, but it runs directly contrary to the agreement itself.
A second motion suggests that new regional development programs and existing regional development programs will be safe. Let me quote from an authority, the Deputy Minister of Finance in the Conservative Government at that time who said:
"We are going to have to think differently in terms of ways to promote
economic development."
That is what he said in response to questions from Members of the Public Accounts Committee. He said:
"The Michelin Tire type of transaction is just not on any more."
He went on to say that: "We will have to find other unobjectionable ways" to provide industrial development assistance. That was his statement to that committee. What
more definite and clear-cut proof could we want than the statement of the Deputy Minister of Finance that we will have to change our regional development programs as a consequence of this trade deal?
Finally, this agreement says a great deal about health care and the future of medicare in this country. If we look at the various services that are provided under the services section of the trade deal, one sees that there are dozens of health services that are not just management services but commercial services that run medical labs, public health labs, and blood banks. All these are being open to national treatment, that is, equal treatment for American firms with Canadian firms.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you have noticed in the past half hour, one Member after another has brought to your attention and to the attention of people watching this debate the fronts on which the Government has failed in negotiating this agreement. It has become gradually evident when examining the Bill.
The Government has failed in protecting aboriginal rights, as the Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) so eloquently put it. It has failed to protect Canadian social security programs as the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) will point out. It has failed on the front of protecting the workers and firms which will be affected by the deal, as other Members will point out.
It has also failed to protect the environment. I will briefly give a chronology of facts to show how, despite the warnings the Government was given, the environment has been neglected.
Despite the fact that the Government published a booklet for almost every activity that comes under federal jurisdiction in which to praise, promote and propagandize the virtues of this agreement, it did not do so with respect to the environment. Not one word was expressed on it. That is, in itself, an astonishing fact. It means that the Government somehow concluded that it would be wiser to say nothing either because conceptually it did not link the agreement with the environment or it felt it was too treacherous a territory on which to speak up on behalf of the Canadian environment.
Let me take you through this chronology, beginning with June, 1986, when the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council alerted the Canadian public to the fact that free trade could have an impact on the environment in Canada. Five months later, in November, 1986, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) came to our committee on the Environment and Forestry to say that although he had requested the report by the Council, he had read it and saw no links between free trade and the environment. The fact that he saw no link was, in itself, an astonishing statement.
August 16, 1988

In 1987, the Minister of the Environment for Canada endorsed the Brundtland Report, which is a very carefully crafted policy paper that speaks about environmentally sustainable development. The Americans have remained silent on this. They have not taken any position on it. Surely at that point, having committed the Government of Canada to the Brundtland Report on the northern side of the border, one would want to make absolutely sure that the commitment would not be eroded by Washington because of its lack of commitment to the very same report.
Let me take you to September, 1987, when the Minister of the Environment endorsed the report of the National Task Force on the Economy and the Environment, which is another emanation of the Brundtland Report. Let us then move to November 23, 1987, when in response to a question of mine on the Order Paper, the Government replied that the free trade agreement is a commercial accord, it is not an environmental agreement.
How blind could one be? How short-sighted can one be for the sake of lower prices, as some of the spokespeople on the other side have said, not to realize that this is not just a commercial agreement? It entails regulations and develops more and more into other measures and legislation that go far beyond commercial operations, as many Members have already indicated this afternoon in the House.
We then come to May, 1988, when an official of the Department of the Environment appeared before the Standing Committee on the Environment and Forestry to deal with the Estimates that came before that committee. We asked him if he conducted any studies on the implications of the agreement on the environment. The answer was that nothing had been undertaken because there was no need to do so. The Minister of the Environment and the Government had decided that trade and the environment are unrelated. Can you believe that, Mr. Speaker? It is unthinkable to have such a short-sighted, blind attitude, if I may say, toward the implication of this agreement.
Another important front that has to be covered by Motion No. 10, which I am addressing now, as proposed by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), is one representing a major shortcoming in the legislation itself. Mr. Speaker, all aspects of life, and the Greeks divided them up into four elements, the earth, the air, water and fire, will be affected by this trade deal. My colleagues have dealt with three of the basic elements, the earth, water and air. I want to deal with the fourth, the fire, the spirit. In other words, culture.
I want to deal with the big lie which the Government has perpetrated with regard to the supposed cultural exemption in the trade deal. We were told that culture would not be on the bargaining table at all. Clearly it was. Clearly the Americans saw a great victory. For them culture is an opportunity for making another buck. It is business as usual. It is entertainment and all of the measures that we have developed as Canadians to promote Canadian culture. To Americans this is discrimination and it is against the spirit of the trade agreement. The Americans would like to have as little of it as possible. Because Canadians are sensitive to the issue, it could not be ignored altogether. We have a double-barrelled exemption for culture. We have a whole lot of areas where cultural industries are very specifically included. I have dealt with them in other speeches.
Here I want to deal with the big lie aspects and the so-called cultural exemption. Let us look at what the Americans say they won in the trade deal negotiations on culture. Recognizing Canadian sensitivities, the U.S. has agreed that certain cultural areas are not subject to special provisions. However, the U.S. retains the right to redress any adverse commercial effects of any future cultural measures enacted by Canada. To them this is just an opportunity to make a buck. If you limit the opportunity for American corporations to make a buck in Canada, that is against the trade deal and the spirit of it, even if it is promoting Canadian creativity and the Canadian cultural world.
We have the chief trade negotiator, Simon Reisman, who has been asked about what this exemption means. The exemption is there in one clause and then there is part 2 of the clause which says there can be retaliation. If Canada does something to promote Canadian culture, the Americans can retaliate. What does Mr. Reisman say about it? He says: "There are many things we can do that would not be inconsistent with the trade deal".
Canada wants to promote Canadian culture in publishing, music, sound recordings, performance, and broadcasting in a particular way, but let us ask the first question. Is it consistent or inconsistent with what we have given away on the trade deal? Unfortunately a lot of it is inconsistent. We have some measures to promote Canadian culture. For example, we have some subsidies. We know that all subsidies are up for negotiation in the next five to seven years. Cultural subsidies are not
exempted there, not at all. We know we have some areas where there is actual protection in foreign investment, for example, in the area of broadcasting. We have Canadian ownership requirements. Canada as a society, and after some considerable thought, decided that it would be better to allow a very small minority of shares to be foreign owned in broadcasting. That is frozen, at least so far in the deal. That is one of the exemptions. But supposing we wanted to do that in some other cultural area-

Hon. Warren AUmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, this evening we are dealing with six Liberal amendments to the free trade Bill, all of which have the purpose for greater certainty of exempting different matters from the Bill.
Motion No. 10 states:
"7. For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall affect programs to protect the environment or conservation of land, resources and waters."
Motion No. 9 has similar provisions for aboriginal lands and aboriginal claims. Motion No. 11 has similar provisions for worker adjustment programs. Motion No. 12 has similar provisions for regional development programs. Motion No. 13 has similar provisions for social and health programs. Motion No. 14 has similar provisions for cultural programs. All these amendments were suggested at the committee by various witnesses appearing before the committee.
For example, the proposal to exempt aboriginal lands and claims was proposed by the Assembly of First Nations. The proposal to exempt environmental protection laws was proposed by the Canadian Environmental Law Association and the Canadian Wildlife Federation. The proposals to exempt regional economic development policy and social programs were proposed by the National Anti Poverty Organizations, GATT-FLY, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, the Canadian Council on Social Development, the Canadian Health Coalition, the "One-Voice Seniors", and Mouvement Solidarity populaire Quebecoise. Finally, the provisions to exempt cultural industries were proposed by ACTRA, the Independent Record Producers, and so on.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
My point is that these motions to amend which are presently before the House came out of hearings from Canadian groups of citizens who very strongly proposed that such measures were put in the Bill. Other members of my Party, and other members in the Opposition are dealing with various of these amendments, but I want to zero in on the ones relating to adjustment policies for Canadian workers and Canadian industry.
There is no doubt that, as a result of the free trade agreement, many jobs will be lost. There have been different studies and different estimates as to how many jobs will be lost, but the fact of the matter is no matter what study is accepted, jobs will be lost. In December, 1987, the former Minister for Employment and Immigration stated that he thought approximately 300,000 jobs would be lost. The next day he reversed himself and withdrew that statement. In 1986, a study conducted by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion stated that approximtely 227,000 jobs would be lost in 17 industries. In a study tabled in December, 1987, the Ontario Department of Labour stated that 280,000 jobs would be at risk in Ontario.
The most recent report of the Economic Council of Canada published on April 13, 1988, stated that there would be a net gain of 250,000 jobs over a 10 year period, but it also stated that there would be a decline of jobs in 17 out of the 36 industries studied. The report of the Economic Council entitled "Venturing Forth", states at page 21: "It indicates clearly that without improvements in Canadian manufacturing productivity, increased United States competition could result in a net decline of output and employment in 17 of the 36 industries studied, virtually all of them in manufacturing". Further on it states: "Some firms will have to merge, others will have to close. As projected in simulation one, for example, the electrical products industry would account for 40 per cent of all of the job losses in manufacturing".
There would be serious losses in manufacturing. The report goes on to say that the employment gains would be in the service industries. It would be, for example, in clerical, sales and services, administrative jobs. We all know that manufacturing jobs, industrial jobs, are generally unionized, highly paid and have benefits and are usually full-time jobs, whereas jobs in the service industries are usually very often part-time and at minimum wage and non-unionized and without benefits. The jobs that we are gaining in this deal on the whole are service type jobs, and the jobs that we are losing are industrial type jobs.
Unfortunately, there is nothing in the agreement and in the Bill which provides for adjustment. The Government launched this whole free trade agreement, it says, as a result of the Royal Commission on the Economic Union and Development Prospects for Canada, known as the Macdonald Report, the Macdonald Royal Commission.

August 16, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
What did Macdonald say? He recommended a free trade agreement, but he also said on page 316 of Volume I of the report: "The commissioner's assessment of the economic costs of free trade indicates that Canadian investors and employees are likely to bear relatively larger adjustment burdens than their United States counterparts. A free trade agreement should therefore incorporate explicit provisions that reflect a proportionately greater cost of adjustment that Canadians will face. It should provide for transitional safeguards which permit temporary limits on the speed of adjustment, and it should operate to smooth out the dislocation and re-employment of workers and physical capital".
That is what was recommended. It was recommended in several other reports, but there are no new adjustment programs. Not only are there no new adjustment programs but the employment and training programs that are presently in place, and have been in place for several years now, have been drastically reduced.
Since 1984, employment and training programs have been reduced by this Conservative Government by 32 per cent. Whereas the budgets were $2.2 billion in 1984, they have now been reduced to $1.5 billion. This is the kind of program that the Government said it is going to rely on to help workers and firms adjust as a result of free trade. That will not do. I pointed out very clearly that there will be serious dislocations of workers. Industrial workers will lose jobs in Hamilton, Cape Breton, Toronto, southern Ontario. Jobs will be opening up in service industries in other areas of the country.
What are we going to do with these middle-aged workers, let us say in the electrical products industry, which will be the worst hit according to the Economic Council report, workers who have spent 20 and 30 years in electrical products industries and all of a sudden they are put out of work and told: "Well, don't be too upset. As a result of this free trade agreement you can have a clerical job out west"? Or, "If you are from central Canada, don't worry. You could have a clerical job or a sales job in Quebec, if you are from Ontario".
Adjustment programs are absolutely necessary. What is surprising is the day after the free trade agreement was tabled in this House, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke to the Canadian Export Association-I believe that is the name of the association-and promised significant and massive adjustment programs. When he returned to the House the following day, we attempted to ask him questions about these programs. We attempted to ask the Minister of Employment about these programs. He said that the Prime Minister was misunderstood.
This is one of the travesties. We oppose the agreement and we think it is a bad agreement. Canada gave much more than it got. It is going to be bad for Canada's independence, identity and sovereignty. Surely, if we are going to have the agreement, there must be provision for adjustment programs. That is why
Motion No. 11, which is presently before us and is one of the six motions, says:
"For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to affect or preclude the continuation of existing or the establishment of new special adjustment programs to help firms or workers ..."

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, the FTA provides a complete arsenal of armaments for large multinationals and right-wing Governments on both sides of the border to bust unions, lower wages, cut social programs, lower environmental standards, cut regional development funding, while simultaneously giving what is know in the agreement as national treatment, or pipeline of resources to the same multinationals for wood, water, minerals, fish and many other things.
I am going to direct my remarks this evening to two key areas covered by the motions before us, one on Motion No. 9, in relation to aboriginal title and rights. 1 must say that I find it unusual that the one Minister of the Crown, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), who clearly under Canada's Constitution and under rulings by the highest courts in Canada, has a fiduciary responsibility to the first citizens and First Nations of Canada, has not participated in the debate and has not produced for the First Nations a report on the impact of the FTA upon those to whom he has a direct constitutional responsibility.
The movement on aboriginal title and rights in Canada since Confederation has been a sorry and sad tale. Perhaps it has been the most sad and sorry in recent decades, going back to 1971-72 with the notorious White Paper which was reversed by the Calder decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, a decision that was tied three-three. That created some movement in the settlement of comprehensive claims but that movement was turned back in 1981-82 when the Government removed aboriginal rights from Canada's Constitution. Of course, we have seen that followed by the now famed Erik Nielsen report known as the Buffalo Jump of the 1980s, a report which would bring about the total assimilation and annihilation of the first citizens of Canada. That, of course, will be followed by the 1988 FTA should it in fact be passed and implemented.
One has to have some understanding of the gravity of the situation affecting first citizens and First Nations to know why the Assembly of First Nations opposed this Bill so strongly before committee and are opposing it so strongly across Canada. This Government has not moved since it came to office on Section 35 of the Constitution, recognizing aboriginal title and rights.
In my view, there is no fair-minded Canadian who is not appalled at the neglect by governments one after another
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
which has brought the First Nations to such a state that any negative social indicator one can imagine can apply including the highest rates of suicide, the lowest rates of employment and the highest rates of incarceration. All the negative social indicators that can be found to measure the situation of the First Nations is there for all to see. The governments have a responsibility to settle comprehensive claims in British Columbia and North of 60 and to live up to the treaties in the rest of Canada. The governments have a responsibility to settle the specific claims which now number over 500.
Those first citizens who are listening this evening have to understand that a premonition of what will come under the FTA was what has gone on in Alberta with the Lubicon people. Just when the federal and provincial Governments could have moved to settle outstanding claims of the Lubicon people, the governments turned over a vast tract of land covering all of the Lubicon claim in northern Alberta to Daishowa Pulp Company, a pulp company wholly owned by Japanese. That process will accelerate, not just in Alberta but in every province and North of 60 should the FTA be implemented.
We must understand what national treatment means. The steeplechases that will have to be jumped by First Nations in order to settle comprehensive claims will be so much higher. One need simply read the FTA to see that local governments would have to follow rules against local preferences.
The First Nations have a true understanding of sustainable development. They understand the Brundtland report, the World Commission on the Environment. They understand how to properly harvest plants, animals and fish. They have a love for the land. One need only read the FTA to see how difficult it will be to maintain that traditional lifestyle.
For example, if an American corporation were to set up a large guiding and outfitting operation next to an Indian band which had a similar operation set up, it would be only a matter of a moment before the parent corporation would take some kind of countervailing action for unfair subsidies against the Indian band. I have here an excellent article entitled "The Binding Dispute Settlement Mechanism". It says:
"And since all Canadian producers are to some extent subsidized by government-run hydro, telephones, postal services, health care systems, etc., etc.-failing US firms will never run out of grounds for filing unfair trade practices suits.
Following a suit brought by the New England fishing industry, for example, the US International Trade Commission identified 58 Canadian government programs it labelled "unfair subsidies" to the Canadian fishing industry."
Let us think for just a moment about long-standing treaty entitlements and the specific entitlements of the first citizens of Canada. How long would it be before they would be challenged before the U.S. International Trade Commission? Even if they were taken before the so-called binding dispute settlement mechanism, we do know this, as stated in the article to which I just referred:

August 16, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
"-binational panels are bound only to US laws and practices whenever US firms want to challenge how we do things in Canada. They have no power to investigate, gather facts, or direct national agencies to make specific judgments. All they can do is judge whether American trade legislation has been applied properly."
The First Nations of Canada perhaps more than any other single identifiable group, stand at risk before the FTA.
I doubt any Member on the government side has read the excellent study done by the Native Council of Canada on the impact of the FTA on the First Nations and first citizens of Canada. We know that the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) has not even read the agreement, so we can be quite certain that the Minister of Indian Affairs has done nothing to date to protect the first citizens.
This motion would simply provide the kind of protection the Government says exists. If it exists, this is precisely the kind of motion the Government should accept to lay to rest the very deep, real and identifiable concerns of the first citizens.
I would like to spend a moment dealing with Motion No. 10. There is another question I want to pose. Why has the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) neither spoken in this debate nor produced for Canadians the estimate of the professionals who are working at Environment Canada of what the impact of the FTA would be?
We know from a recent Canadian Wildlife Service survey that over three-quarters of Canadians are prepared to accept a lower standard of living in order to have a higher quality and a safer environment. Yet south of the border, there has been no serious movement on acid rain. Anyone who has travelled to the Love Canal or to the Niagara Escarpment has seen how the Americans handle waste storage. They drove the locomotive from the atomic testing site to the Niagara Escarpment, simply dug a hole and drove it in. One need only go to Hanford in the State of Washington, just South of British Columbia, to see what American environmental standards are. They simply dump waste onto and into the ground.
When U.S. firms are required to install scrubbers in Canada and there are either federal or provincial incentives to do so, it would be just a blink of an eye before the parent company in the United States brought countervailing action against Canadian firms to try to reduce environmental standards. The Canadian environment stands at enormous risk from the way this agreement is worded, and any Member who truly cares and who truly speaks out on behalf of Canada's environment should support Motion No. 10 to ensure that the environmental standards that all Canadians support will be implemented, maintained and improved in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to speak to this very important series of amendments including Motion Nos. 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 which call the Government's bluff about the take-over that is provided for in the so-called free trade agreement and in Bill C-130.
The rationale for the free trade agreement is that it will reduce tariffs. In fact, that is a very small part of what the agreement really is about. It is partly about giving American corporations a much freer hand than they now have in taking over Canadian resources and Canadian labour.
With regard to the Bill, these amendments attempt to protect the lands, resources, and waters of the aboriginal peoples from the agreement. They attempt to protect environmental and conservation programs for our own land and water. They attempt to protect the continuation of special adjustment programs for workers or companies which suffer under the
agreement. They attempt to protect the establishment or continuation of regional development programs and they attempt to protect the health and social service programs that we have now and the plans and hopes we have for extending them. They attempt to protect our cultural programs, present and future.
It is doubtful, even if these amendments were written in, that that protection would be given because if the free trade deal is finalized the agreement itself would give American corporations claim to all these things. Even if these amendments were written in we would, at the very best, be tied up in long court battles. The Government probably does not want to deal with these amendments because if they are passed it would be caught in contradiction to the agreement it has signed. It does not want to debate the amendments because it knows the amendments expose the take-over provided for by the deal.
I represent a constituency which has at least six hospitals, many nursing homes, and other health institutions, public and private. I want to speak particularly about the amendment which deals with social services. Motion No. 13 would add to the Bill the words:
"-nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to affect the continuation of
existing or the establishment of new Canadian social programs, including
medicare, unemployment insurance, daycare, pensions, minimum wage laws,
labour laws and maternity benefits."
We are being told, of course that these things are not on the table. We were told that by the same Prime Minister who told us that he would never negotiate a free trade deal with the United States. His statement that these are not on the table turns out to be just as true as his promise not to negotiate a free trade deal with the United States.
In fact, under Article 1402 of the agreement any American firm can claim any rights, benefits, and opportunities in Canada which any Canadian firm has under our laws. There can be no preference given to Canadian firms and no preference given to non-profit services over for-profit services.
Under that article these firms will be able to come into Canada much more easily than they now can. The list of nearly 300 services which are expressly opened up includes the management of a series of health services including hospitals, nursing homes, homes for the aged, homes for the retarded, homes for disturbed children, halfway houses, rehabilitation clinics-

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext:

August 16, 1988

This means that as governments deregulate, privatize, and contract out services which are now provided by public servants in a not-for-profit arrangement, they will all become open to takeovers by the American corporations which have established immense financial power and expertise for the purpose of making profit out of people's health. In the United States there are corporations whose large business it is to manage hospitals. They boast that last year and the year before they eliminated 73,000 hospital worker jobs.
In case some naive person on the government side imagines that this is because Americans have become much healthier and do not need hospital care, I will point out that statistics show that many millions of Americans have no hospital care at all, that the time spent by the elderly in particular in these institutions is being reduced, and that the quality of health care in the United States is lower than the quality of health care in Canada, even though the total cost is higher. That is what the Americans get as a result of for-profit hospitals and other services. That is why they want to reduce it here.

People who work at these hospitals, nursing homes, homes for the aged, and other institutions like that now provided as public service under public jurisdiction and control with responsible union relationships among their employees and responsible staffing will be replaced by for-profit groups which in the States, as I have said, have a much lower level of service. I want to read a statement on the implications of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement for Canada's identity and cultural sovereignty. It was issued in July, 1988, and was prepared by the Cultural Industries Alliance composed of the following groups: Alliance of Canadian Cinema, Television and Radio Artists; Association des Producteurs de Film et Video du Quebec; Association of Canadian Film and Television Producers; Association of Canada Film Craftspeople; Association of Canadian Publishers; Canadian Actors' Equity Association; Canadian Association of Motion Picture and Electronic Recording Artists; Canadian Conference of the Arts; Canadian Film and Television Association; Canadian Independent Record Production Association; Canadian Periodical Publishers Association; Directors Guild of Canada; National Association of Broadcast Employees and Technicians; Periodical Writers Association of Canada; and The Writers Union of Canada.
The Alliance states that publishers and writers have allied with actors and directors, as well as with film, television and record producers, to amplify their opposition to the treatment of culture in the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. The singular importance of this issue has persuaded them that they must speak out together to voice their serious concern over the long term effects of the agreement. Each member of this alliance is convinced that the agreement's so-called exemption for culture will actually discourage Canadian Governments in future from taking measures to assist the development of independent cultural industries by Canadians for Canadian audiences.
They believe that nurturing of Canadian works, which reflect and inspire uniquely Canadian points of view, is essential to this country's growth as a sovereign nation. Owing to our small population, our geographic proximity to a major power, and the extraordinary dominance of imported cultural goods, Canadians have found it necessary to provide counterbalances by introducing policies and legislation that make it possible for Canadian voices to be heard in our own country. I would like them to read the Minister's remarks about Canadian voices.
They go on to state that measures that might be taken to ensure this growth, however, appear compromised by the agreement, and it is doubtful if measures introduced in the past would be acceptable were they to be proposed in the post free trade Canada; therefore, they say, we are forced to conclude that our sovereignty is jeopardized by the agreement.

August 16, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
They say that in the past 18 months they have already seen evidence of the effect of the agreement on existing policies and policy development, including: The reduction of the capital cost allowance for Canadian films and television programs, which had encouraged production of Canadian films and television programs;
The revision of the Film Products Importation Act, which now substitutes grants for structural change. The Minister thought she could throw money at the problem and it might go away.
Third is the rejection of the Investment Canada guidelines for film distribution proposed by the 1985 film industry task force, recommendations that would ensure the orderly transfer of ownership in film distribution to Canadians which have been ignored;
Failure to apply the 1985 "Baie Comeau" book publishing policy, which promised to see the transfer of ownership in book publishing to Canadians.
Rejection of key recommendations for broadcast policy made by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. These proposed measures would have significantly enhanced the production of Canadian programs for a Canadian market, and could well have had significant beneficial effects for the recording sector.
They go on to state in their document that it seems clear that the free trade agreement will alter not only the course of our economy, but by inhibiting our freedom to strengthen vulnerable yet essential cultural industries, it will also alter the course of how we define ourselves as Canadians. The agreement recognizes a North American reality, but it leaves little room for a Canadian vision. It is just like the Canadian broadcast Bill introduced by the Minister, which is a sad comment on how she and the Government view the application of a Canadian content policy.
The document states that the Government of Canada has repeatedly offered Canadians the assurance that under the free trade agreement our ability to protect our cultural sovereignty and to provide for the expression of our identity has been protected. For example, in a speech given on April 7, 1988, the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) stated:
"We have a free trade agreement because this Prime Minister, this Minister
of Communications and this Government promised one thing: that Canada's
right to determine our own culture would be respected in every degree.
Without that promise ... a deal simply was not possible."
It is a shame that they did not mean what they said.
The Alliance goes on to say that the organizations which have signed this brief share fully the view expressed by the Minister that no trade agreement is acceptable which does not retain fully Canada's right in the future to take the kinds of measures it has taken in the past to develop its culture. However, they state, all of them have been forced to the conclusion that the free trade agreement of January, 1988, does not meet that test. Instead, the agreement sharply and unacceptably constrains Canada's ability to take the necessary measures in the future to provide fully for the expression of the
values, creativity, ideas and talent of Canadians throughout the country and for such activities to occur under the control of Canadians.
We have concluded as well, they say, based on decisions taken recently by the Government that the Government itself understands that its right of action is substantially limited by the agreement and has been prepared to accept those limits as a cost of the agreement.
What is the evidence on which we base these conclusions? First, we base them on the somewhat convoluted but increasingly understandable formal provisions of the agreement itself.
The key provisions of the Bill are in Article 2005. Rather than repeat those provisions, we simply note that we share the view expressed by Canada's Trade Ambassador and Chief Negotiator, Simon Reisman, that "it is rather impenetrable language". However, in a June 17 speech to the Canadian Film and Television Association, Ambassador Reisman provided considerable help in clarifying what Article 2005 means. He explained that it means:
" ... new measures affecting cultural industries would be scrutinized by both sides to determine whether they were consistent or inconsistent with the agreement."
Let us remember that American law is still American law. We did not change that.
They go on to say that Ambassador Reisman went on to state that if new measures were not consistent with the trade agreement then retaliation of "equivalent commercial value" was provided for. He expressed the opinion that: "There are many things we can do to support the cultural industries without being inconsistent".
Ambassador Reisman's view is clearly different from that of the Minister of Communications, they say. What he is saying, and what we believe the agreement says, is that actions taken in the past are exempt from the agreement, but any new initiatives are not. As a result, all of the provisions in the U.S.-Canada trade agreement which apply to the economy in general apply to the cultural industries as well, insofar as new measures are concerned.
The result is to limit drastically our ability to build our own domestic Canadian-owned and controlled companies in the cultural industries and to further enhance the development of Canadian cultural products. The one area that remains clearly open for government policy is that of direct subsidies. However, we note that the issue of subsidies is itself the subject of a series of negotiations flowing out of the U.S.-Canada trade talks and that, as as result, there is no final resolution of the subsidy issues.
Moreover, there is a need for serious legislative and structural initiatives in the cultural industries, and not just for financial assistance. They go on to state in the document that if we look at the actions the Government has taken in the recent past we see a consistent and profoundly disturbing pattern. The following examples can be cited:

Mr. Speaker, I suppose I should say I am pleased to rise to speak in support of these amendments, but I am also sad to think that we are having this kind of debate and the Government has gone so far as to sell out this country the way it has.
We have heard a lot about the Auto Pact. The Government talks about the Auto Pact as free trade. Anyone who knows anything about trade knows it is very managed trade. In the Auto Pact what we have discussed is the ability to have Canadian content. The Government has eroded that, and the threat to the auto industry is very serious.
We did have a free trade agreement in 1944. It was with the agricultural manufacturing industry entered into with the United States of America. It resulted in a huge deficit in trade and farm machinery. Canada is one of the world's greatest agricultural countries yet we do not manufacture any of our own tractors. That is a specific example of the industrial end of Canada in the future.
More important, I would like to take a few moments to speak about the social policies which the Government is so anxious to say are not in the agreement and have not been touched. We have to look very seriously at the implications. We know that the Government would not get into any kind of discussions about what subsidies are. I am mortified to think that Canadians have negotiated an agreement which leaves everything until later on, later on, later on. I would not want
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
the negotiators negotiating anything else for me because they have not defined what a subsidy is. They say we will get around to it in the next five to seven years. If the United States will have the kind of clout with the government negotiators in the future, we will not have very much say. When we look at what it is costing us in Canada as far as delivering our comprehensive health care system is concerned, which has all sorts of warts in it which need to be improved, we must realize that it happens to be one of the best health systems in the western world and is something of which we should be proud.
The biggest cost per car of General Motors in Detroit is not the steel costs nor the labour costs but the cost of Blue Shield and Blue Cross. It costs General Motors $650 per car in health care delivery.
We know in this country that our labour unit costs have been low because health care costs are built into what it is to be a Canadian and to live in this country. Certainly there is absolutely no reason that cannot be identified as a subsidy when we are talking to industries in the next five to seven years. The insidious part of this is that it is not clear. It is left ambiguous so that we are left as victims with no guarantee about our social policies.
What happens to our unemployment insurance, Mr. Speaker? This is something we thought was a reasonably good program. Again it has its problems. It needs improvements and constantly in this House we review it and try to make it better. We know that people are kept at work and not allowed time off because companies keep trained staff on call while cutting payroll costs. In Canada, 80 per cent of unemployed workers receive unemployment insurance up to 60 per cent of their wages. In the United States only one-quarter of the unemployed receive such benefits, generally at less than 40 per cent of their earnings. Those are the kinds of comparisons we are talking about.
For the Government to say that our social policies are not involved is a lot of nonsense. It says very clearly that we have to harmonize our programs and harmonization means to make things the same. If we are going to make them the same, we have to look at what that means. The greatest treasure we have in Canada is our children. When we talk about their future we have to think about their education. It is very clear that we in Canada have chosen to spend more on elementary and secondary school education per child than in the United States. Is that considered a subsidy?

Mr. Speaker, I also welcome this opportunity to speak in this important debate concerning motions numbered 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14.
My remarks will more specifically concern motions 12 and 13, and especially Motion No. 12, which reads as follows:
"For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to affect or preclude the continuation of existing or the establishment of new regional development programs."
... and now for Motion No. 13, which reads as follows:
"For greater certainty, nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to affect the continuation of existing or the establishment of new Canadian social programs, including medicare, unemployment insurance, daycare, pensions, minimum wage laws, labour laws and maternity benefits."
Mr. Speaker, I listened to all the previous speakers, and I think it is rather astonishing that what we propose in the way of amendments is relatively simple, in the circumstances. The Government is saying: There is no problem, there will be no consequences. What the FTA will do is create jobs and boost growth in this country, and there will be no consequences of any kind.
What we want to do in the House today is improve the Bill by adding a few simple sentences. These additions would provide guarantees that in the circumstances I think are altogether essential, reasonable and indispensable.
We are told that the FTA will have no impact on job creation or regional economic development... so they say! But if they are so sure and spend so much time saying they are so sure, I wonder what their motives are. Why not include guarantees in the FTA so that Canadians know what to expect?
Mr. Speaker, in a survey, American manufacturers were asked what they felt were the ideal conditions for setting up a company. According to the findings of this survey, a good business climate in the various States depended on the following conditions, ranked as follows: low taxes; low union membership; low insurance rates for work-related accidents; low unemployment insurance benefits; low energy costs; and fewer days lost as a result of work stoppages.
Mr. Speaker, if the same survey, evaluation or analysis were made in Canada, the conclusions would obviously be the same.
I think this is the kind of language we can expect from entrepreneurs, from industry, from those who create the jobs. It is quite normal and quite reasonable for a company to want to cut costs. So what will happen when the FTA is implemented? There will be three consequences, Mr. Speaker. There will be howls of "unfair" from the Americans because our conditions will not be the same as theirs. This could affect us in various ways. There might be demands that we "harmonize", over time, various programs that are characteristic of our way of doing things, as opposed to the U.S.

August 16, 1988

However, there is also another possibility, and frankly it worries me, Mr. Speaker, because I talked to various business people, to the people who create jobs, and they often tell us that their American competitors pay an hourly wage of $3, $4, $5 to produce exactly the same goods they are making in Canada. Secondly, he tells us that the labour component of products made in Canada is 30, 35, 40 or 50 per cent of the total.
Mr. Speaker, you have to put yourself in this businessman's place. Obviously, if he cannot have conditions similar to those in the United States, he will be very tempted, very interested, to simply liquidate his business and take an option on some land in the United States, so as to benefit from the almost total lack of social measures on the American side. Who will pick up the tab, Mr. Speaker?
Unfortunately, I have a riding whose survival depends on regional economic development. Before the redistribution of the electoral map, I had 60,000 people in my riding, in 60 municipalities. The largest town had a population of 6,500. Fortunately, with redistribution, I will have 67 municipalities, of which the largest has a population of barely 13,000. Given that, the economic survival of my riding depends on regional development policies and is directly related to them.
In the past, we have seen the benefits-the tremendously positive and essential results-of a regional development policy. In 1982-83, we Liberals put forward a program called Canadian Industrial Renewal Board. It enabled us to develop the Sherbrooke region. This program made it possible to create thousands of jobs, which obviously had a beneficial impact on a riding like mine.
With the treaty before us, Mr. Speaker, we risk losing any regional economic development program.
I think it is interesting and very important as well to recall some figures that I think speak for themselves. You will allow me, Mr. Speaker, to refer, for example, to some self-explanatory numerical data.
We are told that only 25 per cent of the unemployed in the United States receive benefits under all the government and federal programs, as well as supplementary and expanded benefit plans .. . Only 25 per cent! The corresponding figure for Canada is 85 per cent. In the United States, our southern neighbour, unemployment insurance benefits amount on average to 8 per cent of the average wage. In Canada, this average is 40 per cent and even exceeds it in some circumstances. Here we have figures, and I think that to make a case, nothing beats having figures to refer to, real, concrete, actual statistical data.
I think this is a good example of what distinguishes us from our American neighbours. And I also think it is a very good indication of the potential risk of this kind of agreement as a result of transfers of labour and companies that will tend to follow the laws of the market place and set up operations in those states across the border where the minimum wage is
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
much lower and social benefits are far fewer, thus creating an incredible situation in this country. We will lose dozens of companies that will move to the United States, because of the markets and because of the fact that our production costs are much higher, so that companies that stay in Canada will see their premiums for social benefit increase considerably, and so forth. There will be a time when thousands of people are laid off.
Mr. Speaker, there is another aspect I find very significant, and that is the minimum wage. I think the following figures speak for themselves. In Canada, all provinces have a minimum wage policy. When we compare the situation in the United States, we find that nine states have no minimum wage policy; twelve states have a minimum wage of less than S3; and Texas, with the third highest population in the Union, has a minimum wage of SI.40. In Canada, only Alberta has a minimum wage of less than $3. In all other provinces, the minimum wage exceeds $3.
Mr. Speaker, I am not a businessman but, on the basis of this information, if I had to start a business in which the wage component was at all significant, I would be very interested in setting up operations in the United States. The minimum wage is half what it is in this country, there are no social programs, and I am close to my markets. Mr. Speaker, what happens to Canadians who are looking for a job, especially in disadvantaged regions like mine?

What are these amendments, Mr. Speaker? They are amendments that have to do with aboriginal land claims, that would provide that the deal does not affect the special relationship that aboriginal peoples have with the Crown and the federal Government. It seems to me to be a reasonable amendment, not only in terms of the logic of the Government's arguments with respect to amendments, but also with respect to the fact that the Government, in my judgment and in the judgment of aboriginal peoples, has no right to enter into a treaty with another nation that would abrogate rights which they have by virtue of their treaties with the Crown. Surely we would want to make that absolutely clear. Surely it would be an elemental principle of justice in terms of the relationship between native peoples and the Canadian Government that we would want to see enshrined in the legislation implementing the free trade agreement.
Another amendment has to do with the whole question of environmental or conservation programs. If the Government insists, as it does, that this amendment does not affect environmental or conservation programs, what on earth could be wrong with an amendment that says so? What could be wrong with an amendment that makes explicit what the Government itself argues is already the case, unless what the Government argues is the case is a matter of interpretation, or a matter of trying to sell the agreement politically when the Government knows full well that many of these types of programs could come to be the object of negotiation between Canada and the United States.
